Section.Description: The recommended exposure limit (REL) is the maximum amount or concentration of a chemical that a worker may be exposed to.  The RELs are guidelines established and recommended by the NIOSH (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health).  The RELs can be given in three ways. [1] Time-weighted average (REL-TWA): average exposure based on up to10h/day, 40h/week work schedule. [2] Short-term exposure limit (REL-STEL): a 15-minute TWA exposure that should not be exceeded at any time during a workday. [3] Ceiling limit (REL-C): absolute exposure limit that should not be exceeded at any time.

The permissible exposure limit (PEL) is the maximum amount or concentration of a chemical that a worker may be exposed to under OSHA regulations.  The PEL can be given in three ways. [1] Time-weighted average (PEL-TWA): average exposure based on an 8h/day, 40h/week work schedule. [2] Short-term exposure limit (PEL-STEL): a 15-minute TWA exposure that should not be exceeded at any time during a workday. [3] Ceiling limit (PEL-C): absolute exposure limit that should not be exceeded at any time.

Section.TOCHeading: Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health (IDLH)
Section.Description: The Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health air concentration values (IDLH values) characterize high-risk exposure concentrations and conditions and are used as a component of respirator selection criteria.  IDLH values are established (1) to ensure that the worker can escape from a given contaminated environment in the event of failure of the respiratory protection equipment and (2) to indicate a maximum level above which only a highly reliable breathing apparatus, providing maximum worker protection, is permitted.

The threshold limit value (TLV) of a chemical is an airborne concentration at which a worker can be exposed day after day for a working lifetime without adverse effect.  There are three types of TLVs for chemicals. [1] Threshold limit value - time-weighted average (TLV-TWA): average exposure on the basis of a 8h/day, 40h/week work schedule. [2] Threshold limit value - short-term exposure limit (TLV-STEL): a 15-minute TWA exposure that should not be exceeded at any time during a workday, even if the 8-hour TWA is within the TLV-TWA. [3] Threshold limit value - ceiling limit (TLV-C): absolute exposure limit that should not be exceeded at any time. TLVs are developed by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienist.  While TLVs are widely accepted occupational exposure limits, they are not standards enforced by the U.S. Government.

StringWithMarkup.String: N-isopropylaniline (CAS # 768-52-5) was evaluated for acute inhalation toxicity in groups of Sprague-Dawley rats (5/sex/group) exposed for 4 hours in an inhalation chamber to mean analytical concentrations of 1.4, 1.4, 1.3, 1.0 mg/L vapor/aerosol in air. Mortality associated with treatment was consistent with an LC50 (probit) of 1.2 mg/L in air. Rats of a 1.0 mg/L exposure showed neither overt signs of toxicity nor diminished weight gain, while all other treated groups exhibited a transient decrease in mean bodyweights on Day 2 following exposures. Hypoactivity and respiratory distress or irritation were the most oft reported clinical irregularities during 14-day post-exposure observation. Necropsy of both surviving and decedent rats revealed no treatment-related pathology.

StringWithMarkup.String: N-isopropylaniline (CAS # 768-52-5) was evaluated for subchronic dermal toxicity in Sprague-Dawley rats (10/sex/group) exposed by non-occluded dermal applications upon shaved skin (approximately 10% of total body surface area) to target doses of 0 (negative control), 25, 100, and 400 mg/kg/day, 5 days/week x 4 weeks. A study simulation established 30% loss of test material to volatilization by this method. Treatment was associated with statistically significant reduction in cumulative bodyweight gain and reduced 1st week feed consumption in high dose males relative to controls, but no mortality. Primarily middle and high dose females exhibited dryness, redness, abrasions, and/or scabbing at the treatment sites, although dermal irritation was evident at all exposure levels in both sexes. Dose-related occurrences of anemia and methemoglobinemia were statistically significant (Dunnett's T, p < 0.05) in high and mid-dose rats of both sexes, as splenic changes (increased relative and absolute weight, hematopoiesis, and hemosiderin accumulation) were in high dose animals. Acanthosis (epidermal thickening) was also observed in all treated males and females of the two highest doses. Enlargement of the submaxillary lymph node with hyperplasia on histopathologic examination was regarded as secondary to treatment-induced skin lesions. The authors concluded that treatment-related elevations of reticulocyte counts and increased hemosiderin pigment in the spleen suggests toxic anemia by increased red blood cell destruction with compensating activity in both the spleen and bone marrow, rather than reduced production by the bone marrow.

StringWithMarkup.String: N-isopropylaniline (CAS # 768-52-5) was evaluated for subchronic inhalation toxicity in Sprague-Dawley rats (15/sex/group) exposed in an inhalation chamber to mean analytical concentrations of 0, 5.3, 20, and 100 mg/cu m, 6 hours/day, 5 days/week x approximately 14 weeks. Following gross necropsy, only liver and kidneys of high dose animals and spleens of all treated and control animals were submitted for microscopic examination. Throughout study, no deaths or clinical toxicity were attributable to treatment, while weight gains were reduced from second week of treatment to terminal necropsy. Males and females of all exposure levels also exhibited statistically significant (Dunnett's T, p < 0.05) dose-related methemoglobinemia, with elevated methemoglobin levels ranging from 56 to 344% over those in controls; slight (6% or less) but statistically significant anemia was noted in high-dose animals of both sexes. Gross pathology included slight increases in relative kidney and spleen weights on terminal necropsy. Microscopically, all high exposure animals exhibited increased splenic hemosiderin levels. Universal methemoglobinemia in treated rats precluded calculation of a NOEL in this study.

StringWithMarkup.String: N-isopropylaniline (CAS # 768-52-5) was evaluated for subchronic inhalation toxicity in Sprague-Dawley rats (15/sex/group) exposed in inhalation chambers to mean analytical concentrations of 0, 0.055, 0.16, and 0.49 mg/L of air, 6 hours/day, on 21 days over a 4-week period. No treatment-related mortality occurred throughout 21-day study. During exposure, high dose animals of both sexes exhibited hypoactivity and lacrimation, while observations of oral and nasal drainage and encrustation, salivation, and lacrimation were dose-related. High dose animals of both sexes weighed less throughout the study. Dose-related methemoglobinemia at all exposure levels and anemia of high dose males and females were statistically significant (two-tailed Dunnett's T, p < 0.05) by both Coulter and CO-oximeter, the methemoglobinemia levels increasing 3.5% between interim and terminal determinations with continued high level exposures. Red blood cell counts and hematocrit values were significantly (p < 0.01) diminished in high dose males and mid and high dose females. Study authors interpreted these findings, with significantly elevated bilirubin levels (0.49 mg/L) in the absence of detectable liver disease, as indicative of mild hemolytic activity. Mild to moderate reticulocytosis was also significant (p < 0.05 in mid dose males, p < 0.01 in all others) in mid and high dose males and females. Upon terminal necropsy, both absolute and relative spleen weights were significantly elevated in high- and mid-level exposed males and females. Congestion and increased hematopoiesis characterized the splenic lesions in these groups and 4 females of 0.055 mg/L N-isopropylaniline exposures. Additionally, females of mid and high exposures consistently exhibited nephrosis with regeneration in the para recta, while males of all exposure levels showed random renal cortical lesions ranging in severity from nephrosis with regenesis to nephropathy. A NOEL for N-isopropylaniline was not identified in this study.

StringWithMarkup.String: N-Isopropylaniline's production and use as a dye and chemical intermediate may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. N-Isopropylaniline is also a metabolite from the microbial degradation of the herbicide propachlor. If released to air, an estimated vapor pressure of 0.44 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates isopropylaniline will exist solely as a vapor in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase N-isopropylaniline will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 6 hours. Direct photolysis may also occur, but the kinetics of this reaction are unknown. If released to soil, N-isopropylaniline is expected to have low mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 566. A pKa value of 5.3 suggests that N-isopropylaniline will partially exist in the protonated form in aqueous environments and the protonated form of N-isopropylaniline is expected to bind strongly to soil surfaces. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is expected to be an important fate process for the neutral species based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 7.4X10-6 atm-cu m/mole. N-Isopropylaniline is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces based upon its vapor pressure. If released into water, N-isopropylaniline is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment in water based upon the estimated Koc. Volatilization from water surfaces is expected to be an important fate process for the neutral species based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. Estimated volatilization half-lives for a model river and model lake are 4 and 47 days, respectively. An estimated BCF of 17 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Occupational exposure to N-isopropylaniline may occur through inhalation and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where N-isopropylaniline is produced or used. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
